title: Chiasmal Syndromes & Junctional Scotoma: A Clinical Masterclass
summary: A comprehensive guide to the neuro-ophthalmology of the optic chiasm, focusing on the localization of lesions, the mechanism of junctional scotoma, and the multi-disciplinary management of sellar masses.

sections.title: Defining the Chiasm
sections.content: The optic chiasm is a 12mm x 8mm x 4mm structure where approximately 53% of optic nerve fibers (nasal retinal fibers) decussate to the contralateral optic tract. It is situated in the suprasellar cistern, typically 10mm superior to the pituitary gland, allowing for significant tumor growth before visual symptoms manifest.

sections.title: The Junctional Scotoma (Von Willebrand's Knee)
content: Step 1: Lesion involves the posterior aspect of one optic nerve at its junction with the chiasm.
Step 2: Damage to ipsilateral fibers results in a central scotoma in the ipsilateral eye.
Step 3: Compression of the 'Wilbrand Knee'—inferonasal fibers from the contralateral eye that loop 1-2mm into the ipsilateral optic nerve before heading to the tract.
Step 4: Result: Ipsilateral central scotoma + Contralateral superior temporal quadrant defect.

rows: Temporal defect in one eye, sparing the other

sections.title: The 'Hemifield Slide' Phenomenon
sections.content: Patients with bitemporal hemianopia lose the overlapping binocular visual field. This causes the two remaining nasal hemifields to 'slide' relative to each other, leading to diplopia, difficulty with near tasks (threading a needle), and loss of depth perception, even without strabismus.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): Present if compression is asymmetric.
Optic Atrophy: Often 'Bow-tie' or 'Band' atrophy in the eye with temporal field loss.
See-Saw Nystagmus: One eye elevates and intorts while the other eye depressess and extorts; often seen with large parasellar tumors.
Color Vision: Dyschromatopsia often precedes visual acuity loss.
Ocular Motility: Check for CN III, IV, or VI palsies (suggests cavernous sinus invasion).

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Pituitary Apoplexy
content: Sudden, excruciating 'Thunderclap' headache
Rapidly progressive vision loss or ophthalmoplegia
Altered mental status or meningismus
Acute adrenal insufficiency (Hypotension, Electrolyte imbalance)
Nausea and projectile vomiting

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: 1. Formal Visual Fields (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2).
2. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) of RNFL and Ganglion Cell Complex (GCC).
3. MRI Brain and Orbits with and without Gadolinium (Coronal/Sagittal thin cuts of Sella).
4. Comprehensive Endocrine Panel (Prolactin, GH, Cortisol, ACTH, TSH, T4, LH/FSH).
5. Neurosurgical Consultation.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Most common chiasmal tumor in children: Optic Pathway Glioma (OPG).
Strong association with Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) in 15-70% of cases.
Clinical triad: Vision loss, nystagmus, and endocrine dysfunction (Precocious puberty).
Craniopharyngioma is the most common non-glial pediatric sellar tumor.

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Pearls
content: The 'Wilbrand Knee' Controversy: Some modern studies suggest it is an artifact of monocular enucleation in old specimens, yet junctional scotoma remains a definitive clinical localization tool.
Post-Op VF: Visual field recovery can begin within hours of surgical decompression.
OCT Prediction: Ganglion Cell Inner Plexiform Layer (GCIPL) thickness is often a better predictor of post-surgical visual recovery than RNFL.
Pseudo-Chiasmal Defect: Tilted discs or sector retinitis pigmentosa can mimic bitemporal defects (check if defects respect the vertical midline).

sections.title: Recent Advances: Neuroprotection
sections.content: Recent studies in landmark journals investigate the role of systemic neuroprotective agents (like Erythropoietin or Citicoline) as adjuncts to surgery to maximize the recovery of 'dormant' axons that have been chronically compressed but are not yet atrophic.
